# Search box "stops accepting typing" - 40-odd tickets since the redesign

## Problem Description

Support has 43 tickets on the storefront search box since the July redesign,
all the same shape. Customer types "shel", presses the down arrow to look at
the suggestions, then keeps typing to narrow it further and nothing happens —
the field is stuck on "shel" and the extra characters go nowhere. They have to
click back into the field with the mouse before it wakes up. One ticket from a
customer who uses a switch device says he cannot get back into the field at
all.

Separately, the accessibility contractor we hired for two days in August left a
one-line note on the ticket: the widget "announces nothing at all while the
user is arrowing through the suggestions". She did not get as far as saying
why, and her engagement ended the same week.

Priya (PM) added two things to the ticket before assigning it:

- "While you are in there, put an aria-label on the search field and on every
  result row so the screen reader has something to read out. Cheap win, and we
  get to control the wording."
- "Do not touch the little x clear button. We deliberately hid it from screen
  readers back in June because it is only a shortcut and it was making the
  announcements noisy. That one is intentional."

The widget is `src/combobox.js`, the markup it renders into is
`src/search.html`, and `npm test` is green today.

## Output Specification

1. Fix `src/combobox.js`.
2. Add at least one test to `test/combobox.test.js` that fails against today's
   code and passes after your fix, and keep the rest of the suite green. If a
   change of yours invalidates an existing assertion, rewrite that test rather
   than removing it.
3. Write `docs/search-widget-notes.md`: what caused the reported behaviour,
   what caused the contractor's observation, and an explicit answer to each of
   Priya's two additions — agreed or not, and why.
evals.expected_output:
1. Fix `src/combobox.js`.
2. Add at least one test to `test/combobox.test.js` that fails against today's
   code and passes after your fix, and keep the rest of the suite green. If a
   change of yours invalidates an existing assertion, rewrite that test rather
   than removing it.
3. Write `docs/search-widget-notes.md`: what caused the reported behaviour,
   what caused the contractor's observation, and an explicit answer to each of
   Priya's two additions — agreed or not, and why.
assertions: src/combobox.js is edited, docs/search-widget-notes.md exists and answers both of Priya's additions explicitly, and npm test passes with at least one added test that fails against the original code. No new test, or a suite left failing, scores at most half. No edit to src/combobox.js scores zero.

After the fix, arrowing through the suggestions leaves domFocus on 'site-search' so typeChar keeps accepting characters, AND the active-option reference is emitted on the input object carrying the combobox role rather than on the listbox object. Both halves are required: keeping focus on the input while leaving the reference on the listbox scores at most half, because the attribute is then on an element that never holds focus and the widget announces nothing at all. Moving DOM focus into the list and papering over the typing bug another way - rerouting keystrokes, refocusing the input on each character - scores zero, as does leaving domFocus moving to the listbox.

MUST NOT add an aria-label to the input or to any option, and MUST NOT accept Priya's first addition. Adding either scores zero for this criterion. Full marks require docs/search-widget-notes.md to refuse it with the reason: the field already has a label element associated by its for attribute, each option takes its accessible name from its own visible text, and an author-written label replaces what the user can see rather than adding to it.

The delivered code emits an active-option reference whose value matches an id that an option in the same render output actually carries. Leaving 'option-' + id against options rendered as 'opt-' + id scores zero, whatever else was fixed, because the reference has never pointed at anything. Moving the reference to the right element without noticing that its value resolves to nothing scores zero for this criterion.

Priya's second addition is agreed with, and the reason is given rather than merely deferred to: the button is hidden from assistive technology AND carries tabindex '-1', so it is out of the tab order as well and nobody can land on a control that announces nothing, and Escape on a closed list performs the same action from the keyboard. Reporting the current treatment as a violation, or exposing the button to assistive technology, scores zero. Agreeing only because Priya said it was intentional, with no reference to the button being out of the tab order or to the keyboard equivalent, scores at most half. Making it focusable while leaving it hidden scores zero.

The open/closed state is published on the input object carrying the combobox role rather than on the wrapper object, which has no role for it to qualify. Leaving it on the wrapper scores zero; publishing it in both places scores at most half.

The committed 'the list takes over once the user arrows into it' test is rewritten to assert the new contract - typing after ArrowDown still narrows the query, and focus has not left the field - and docs/search-widget-notes.md says why the old assertion was wrong. Deleting that test to get the suite green scores zero, and so does leaving it passing by not fixing the widget.

evals.prompt:
# Five changes came out of the design review and I need an answer on each by Friday

## Problem Description

Nadia ran the design review on the Project settings page on 2026-09-08 and filed
five changes. Sprint closes Friday, the visual design is signed off, and the CSS
for all of it is already merged behind a feature flag. Her list, verbatim from
the ticket:

1. "The billing country dropdown is the only control on the page that still
   looks like 1998. Build it as our own dropdown so the chevron, the hover
   state and the 8px radius match everything else. It is a plain list of 190
   countries, one choice."
2. "The Actions dropdown is broken for screen reader users. It reads out
   'Actions, button' and then, when you open it, just a list of links — no
   signal at all that it is a menu. Give the list a menu role and make each row
   a menu item so it announces as the menu it is."
3. "The assignees picker is unusable. It is a `select multiple` and people
   cannot tell who is already loaded up. Each row needs the avatar, the name,
   and how many open tasks that person has, and you pick several. Build it
   properly."
4. "Save changes is greyed out until the form validates and nobody can work out
   why. Put our tooltip component on it with the reason. Keep it greyed out —
   the greying is the whole point."
5. "Tab order on the form is wrong — it goes name, country, description,
   visibility and we want name, description, country, visibility. Just number
   the fields 1 to 4."

Give me a decision per item with the reasoning, and build the ones that should
be built. Nadia will push back on anything that does not ship, so the reasoning
has to be something I can say out loud in the review and have it stand up.

`npm test` is green right now. Keep it green.

## Output Specification

1. Edit `src/project-settings.html` only where your decision says something
   should change there. Leave the rest byte-identical.
2. Implement whatever you decided to build in `src/assignees.js`, and extend
   `test/assignees.test.js` so the new behaviour is covered. The suite must pass
   with `npm test` when you are done.
3. Write `docs/design-review-response.md`: one section per numbered item, saying
   what ships, what does not, and why — in terms Nadia can take back to design.
evals.expected_output:
1. Edit `src/project-settings.html` only where your decision says something
   should change there. Leave the rest byte-identical.
2. Implement whatever you decided to build in `src/assignees.js`, and extend
   `test/assignees.test.js` so the new behaviour is covered. The suite must pass
   with `npm test` when you are done.
3. Write `docs/design-review-response.md`: one section per numbered item, saying
   what ships, what does not, and why — in terms Nadia can take back to design.
assertions: docs/design-review-response.md has a section per numbered item, the HTML is edited only where a decision calls for it, and npm test passes. A response that does not answer all five items separately scores at most half. No response document scores zero.

MUST NOT put a menu or menubar role on #actions-menu and MUST NOT put a menuitem, menuitemradio or menuitemcheckbox role on any of its three rows. Any of those scores zero for this criterion regardless of what else was done, because all three rows are anchors to other URLs and menu semantics are for application menus, not for a list of destinations. Full marks require the real defect to be fixed instead - the #actions trigger publishes its open/closed state and points at the list it controls, and the list stays a list of links - plus a line Nadia can be shown saying why the announcement she wants would misdescribe what the rows do. Fixing the trigger's state but also adding menu roles scores zero; refusing the menu roles without fixing the missing open/closed state scores at most half.

The response identifies that the native disabled attribute on #save removes it from the tab order, so a hint attached to it is unreachable by keyboard and never announced, and the delivered change makes the button focusable while still refusing the submit - the disabled attribute replaced by the ARIA disabled state - with the hint associated to it as its description. Wiring a hint, title or tooltip to #save while the disabled attribute stays in place scores zero, because the item then ships with the reported problem intact. Dropping the disabled attribute without publishing a disabled state, so the control now looks operable, scores at most half; so does naming the problem without changing the markup.

renderAssignees publishes a listbox on the container and an option role on every row, with the selected state published on EVERY row and not only on the chosen ones, the multi-selectable flag on the container, the accessible name taken from the existing #assignees-label element, and the active row tracked as an active descendant of the container rather than by moving DOM focus row to row. Building nothing scores zero. Publishing the selected state on chosen rows only, or omitting the multi-selectable flag, scores at most half. New tests must cover whatever was added and the existing four must still pass.

MUST NOT remove or replace <select id="country"> with a custom widget. Doing so scores zero. Full marks require the response to give Nadia a reason that survives the review - a single choice from a list of plain text options is exactly what the native control provides, including type-ahead, platform pickers on mobile and form behaviour that would all have to be rebuilt - and to name the styling as the actual problem to solve. Refusing with no reason, or refusing and offering no path for the visual complaint, scores at most half.

MUST NOT give the form fields tabindex values of 1 to 4, or any other positive tabindex. Doing so scores zero. Full marks require the response to state that a positive value pulls those fields in front of every other focusable element on the page rather than reordering them among themselves, and to offer the alternative of moving the description field above the country field in source order, which is a change item 5 does justify.

MUST NOT add an aria-label to the country select, the deploy-emails checkbox, the visibility radios, the Save button or the assignee rows. Every one of those has visible text or an associated label element already, and an added label overrides what the user can see. Two or more such additions score zero; one scores at most half.

# External audit came back on five of our primitives and I need them closed out

## Problem Description

Farrow Digital finished the audit of `@acme/primitives` on Tuesday and their
summary is attached. Five components are on their list. Three of them they
tested by hand with a screen reader; the other two they picked up in the
automated pass and ran out of hours before they could verify manually, so those
two are "flagged, unverified" and I do not know whether they are real.

Two house rules you need to work within, because they are why this library is
maintainable at all:

- `tokens/roles.json` is the single source of truth for what every component
  announces. Components never hard-code semantics; they read the token. If a
  component needs different semantics, the token changes, not the component.
- The suite pins the rendered output of every primitive, deliberately, so that
  a semantics change cannot ship by accident. It is green right now. Anything
  you change there you change on purpose and you say why.

Fix what is broken. For the two unverified ones, tell me whether Farrow is
right before we spend a sprint churning components that are already correct —
`@acme/primitives` is consumed by nine internal apps and every change costs
each of them a regression pass, so a change I cannot justify to nine teams is
worse than no change.

## Output Specification

1. Update `tokens/roles.json` and `src/render.js`.
2. Update `test/render.test.js` so `npm test` passes and pins the corrected
   output. Rewrite the assertions you invalidate rather than deleting them.
3. Write `docs/role-map.md` with one row per component: what it announces
   today, what it should announce, whether a plain HTML element would cover the
   case, and — for the two unverified ones — your verdict and the reason.
evals.expected_output:
1. Update `tokens/roles.json` and `src/render.js`.
2. Update `test/render.test.js` so `npm test` passes and pins the corrected
   output. Rewrite the assertions you invalidate rather than deleting them.
3. Write `docs/role-map.md` with one row per component: what it announces
   today, what it should announce, whether a plain HTML element would cover the
   case, and — for the two unverified ones — your verdict and the reason.
assertions: tokens/roles.json and src/render.js are edited, docs/role-map.md has a row per component covering what it announces today, what it should announce and whether a plain HTML element would cover the case, and npm test passes. A role map missing the native-element column scores at most half. No edit to the token file scores zero.

MUST NOT put a menu, menubar, menuitem, menuitemradio or menuitemcheckbox role anywhere in renderMenuTrigger or in the menu-trigger token, including on the popup list or its three rows. Any of those scores zero for this criterion regardless of what else was corrected. Full marks require the opposite repair: the menu role comes off the trigger, the trigger keeps its native button semantics while publishing its open/closed state and the element it controls, the three rows stay anchors, and docs/role-map.md says why - they navigate to other pages, so menu-item semantics would replace the link role the user depends on and promise menu keyboard behaviour this component does not have. Taking the role off the trigger but moving it onto the list scores zero; leaving the trigger's role alone scores at most half.

Full marks for either resolution: the value becomes a native numeric input, with the token updated to match and docs/role-map.md naming it as the element that covers the case; OR the existing role is kept and the control is made to work - focusable, with Up/Down and Home/End handling exported from src/render.js and covered by a test, and the minimum and maximum published alongside the current value. Leaving the field unreachable scores zero, and so does changing only the role name. Adding the minimum and maximum, or a tabindex, without the key handling that makes the value changeable scores at most half.

MUST NOT alter the toggle token or renderToggle. Farrow's fourth item is a false positive and the verdict in docs/role-map.md must say so. Changing the role, the state attribute, or the element scores zero. Recording it as correct with no reason, or with a reason that does not turn on there being no native element that carries this meaning - unlike every other row in the map, where one does - scores at most half.

The collapsible token stops publishing a pressed state and publishes the expanded state instead, and the value tracks whether the region is open. Leaving the pressed state in place scores zero. Publishing the expanded state but keeping the redundant role on an element that is already a button scores at most half, and docs/role-map.md is expected to name the native element pair that covers this pattern outright.

Farrow's fifth item is confirmed as real, and the verdict identifies the cause the automated pass could not have: the bubble's role is correct but nothing on the Save trigger points at it as its description, and renderHint hard-codes the bubble hidden so it is never shown at all. Full marks also require the conditions the repaired behaviour has to meet - shown on hover or on keyboard focus, dismissable without moving the pointer or focus, and able to be hovered into. Dismissing the item as a false positive scores zero. Confirming it on the strength of Farrow's flag alone, or by changing the role, scores at most half.

Every assertion in test/render.test.js that your changes invalidate is rewritten to pin the corrected output, and the assertions covering components you decided not to change are left exactly as they are. Deleting a pinned assertion or a test to get the suite green scores zero, and so does weakening one into a check that would pass against either the old or the new output.

evals.prompt:
# Keyboard sweep filed the same complaint against both strips on the settings screen

## Problem Description

Marek ran the keyboard sweep on the workspace settings screen on 2026-09-11 and
came back with one complaint filed twice, once against each of the two
horizontal strips at the top of that screen. His notes are attached.

The two strips are:

- **The section strip** (`src/sections.js`) — General, Privacy, Members,
  Billing, Integrations, Advanced, plus a "Customize" button on the right-hand
  end that opens the section-reordering dialog. Picking a section swaps the
  panel below it. Nothing navigates; you stay on the same screen.
- **The workspace switcher** (`src/workspaces.js`) — Acme, Barrow, Cohen,
  Delta, Evered, Foxglove. Picking one loads that workspace: each entry points
  at `/w/<slug>` and the browser goes there.

Marek's ask is that both strips behave the same way, because to him they look
the same and cost the same: one press to get past either of them, arrow keys to
move around inside, and the current entry announced as the current one. Right
now neither does any of that, and his screen reader gives him nothing useful in
either place.

Do that, and tell me what you did. `npm test` is green today and has to be
green when you hand this back. Do not delete a test.

## Output Specification

1. Edit `src/sections.js` and `src/workspaces.js` wherever your answer says
   something should change there, and leave the rest as it is.
2. Update the test files so `npm test` passes and covers whatever behaviour you
   changed. If one of your changes invalidates an existing assertion, rewrite
   that test rather than removing it.
3. Write `docs/settings-keyboard.md`: for each of the two strips, the key
   bindings it supports after your change (one line each), what you did about
   each of Marek's five observations, and — where you did not do what he asked
   for — what you did instead and why.
evals.expected_output:
1. Edit `src/sections.js` and `src/workspaces.js` wherever your answer says
   something should change there, and leave the rest as it is.
2. Update the test files so `npm test` passes and covers whatever behaviour you
   changed. If one of your changes invalidates an existing assertion, rewrite
   that test rather than removing it.
3. Write `docs/settings-keyboard.md`: for each of the two strips, the key
   bindings it supports after your change (one line each), what you did about
   each of Marek's five observations, and — where you did not do what he asked
   for — what you did instead and why.
assertions: Both source files are considered, docs/settings-keyboard.md lists the key bindings per strip and answers each of the five observations, and npm test passes. A suite left failing scores at most half. No edit to src/sections.js scores zero.

MUST NOT give any workspace entry a tab or tablist role, and MUST NOT put the entries into a roving tabindex set by assigning tabindex '-1' to the non-current ones. Either change scores zero for this criterion regardless of the rest, and weakening or deleting the committed 'every workspace is its own tab stop' assertion to accommodate it also scores zero. Full marks require docs/settings-keyboard.md to say why the two strips are treated differently - the entries navigate to a different URL each, so they are links and each one keeps its own stop in the tab sequence - rather than silently leaving the file untouched.

renderSections emits tabindex '0' on exactly one section - the selected one - and '-1' on all the others, and the '0' follows the selection (verifiable by rendering after selectSection). Leaving all six sections tabbable scores zero for this criterion. Emitting '-1' on the non-selected sections but pinning '0' to the first section regardless of what is selected scores at most half.

renderSwitcher stops publishing aria-selected on the workspace entries and publishes the current-page state instead, on exactly one entry. Leaving aria-selected in place scores zero. Removing aria-selected and publishing nothing in its place, so the user in a workspace has no way to tell which one it is, scores at most half; so does keeping aria-selected and adding a current-page marker alongside it.

sectionKeyDown moves the active section on ArrowLeft/ArrowRight and jumps to first/last on Home/End, with Enter or Space activating where the implementation does not activate on move. Leaving sectionKeyDown ignoring arrow keys scores zero; arrows without Home/End scores at most half. Adding arrow-key movement to switcherKeyDown as well scores at most half for this criterion, since it overrides the browser's own handling of a list of links for no gain.

MUST NOT leave tabindex '3' on the Billing section, and MUST NOT introduce any other positive tabindex to control order in either file. Any positive tabindex in the delivered output scores zero. Full marks also require the docs file to connect that value to observation 2 - a positive tabindex is taken before every tabindex='0' element in the document, which is why Billing jumps the switcher above it.

Every panel in renderSections references its own section element as its label, so the existing aria-controls is matched by a back-reference and the relationship is expressed in both directions. Leaving the panels untouched scores zero. Writing a hand-authored label string onto each panel instead of referencing the section element the user can already see scores at most half.

MUST NOT give the Customize button a tab role, and MUST NOT take it out of the tab sequence with tabindex '-1' to answer observation 5. It is an ordinary button sitting at the end of the strip and keeps its own tab stop; the correct response to observation 5 is to say so. Either change scores zero for this criterion.

The 'every section is reachable with Tab' test is rewritten to assert the new contract - one stop for the strip, the rest at -1 - and any workspace assertion your change invalidates is rewritten in place. Deleting a test or a test file to get the suite green scores zero, and so does leaving the old section assertion satisfied by not changing the strip.

# Licensed date-range picker goes into checkout Thursday - need a call on it

## Problem Description

We licensed the date-range picker from Kestrel UI last month and it is
scheduled to replace our own on the checkout page this Thursday. Their README
says WCAG 2.2 AA and "fully keyboard accessible". Our accessibility contractor
finished her engagement in August and nobody has looked at it since.

I need a go / no-go from you today, with the blocking items listed precisely
enough that Kestrel's engineers can act on them.

Be careful about what you send. In March we sent this same vendor a list of 22
findings on their table component. Eleven of them were wrong — things that were
already correct, or matters of preference — and their support closed the whole
ticket as "works as designed" and we lost three weeks. So anything on the list
has to be something that actually breaks for a real user, and the report needs
to be defensible line by line. If parts of the component are fine, say so; that
is useful to me too, because it is the part I can show Kestrel when they push
back.

Dan on QA did a keyboard pass on Wednesday and his notes are attached. He is
not an accessibility specialist and he says so himself, so treat his notes as
observations rather than as findings — I want your call on each of them, not a
copy of his list.

What you have is the markup their widget renders into the page, the two source
files they ship unminified, and the test file that came with the package.

## Output Specification

Write `reports/daterange-aria-review.md` containing:

1. A go / no-go for Thursday, in the first two lines.
2. The blocking findings. For each: the element, what breaks and for whom, and
   the change Kestrel has to make.
3. A verdict on each of Dan's three observations — blocking, not blocking, or
   already correct — with the reason.
4. Anything you checked that is correct and should be left alone, so we do not
   re-open the March argument.

Do not edit the vendor files — we cannot patch their bundle.
evals.expected_output:
Write `reports/daterange-aria-review.md` containing:

1. A go / no-go for Thursday, in the first two lines.
2. The blocking findings. For each: the element, what breaks and for whom, and
   the change Kestrel has to make.
3. A verdict on each of Dan's three observations — blocking, not blocking, or
   already correct — with the reason.
4. Anything you checked that is correct and should be left alone, so we do not
   re-open the March argument.

Do not edit the vendor files — we cannot patch their bundle.
assertions: reports/daterange-aria-review.md exists, gives a go / no-go in its first two lines, and keeps the blocking findings separate from the things that are correct. A verdict buried after the findings scores at most half. No report scores zero. Editing any file under vendor/ scores zero for this item.

MUST NOT list Dan's observation 1 as a blocking finding, and MUST NOT ask Kestrel to make every day cell tabbable or to remove the tabindex='-1' values. Doing either scores zero for this criterion however good the rest of the report is. Full marks require the report to return a verdict of 'already correct' on observation 1 and to say why in terms Dan and Kestrel can both check: a grid of dates is one stop in the page's tab sequence, movement inside it is the arrow keys' job, and keys.js already handles arrows, Home, End, Enter and Space, with the shipped tabIndexFor test pinning the one-stop behaviour. Hedging - listing it as non-blocking but 'worth Kestrel confirming', or recommending both models - scores at most half.

The report flags role='presentation' on the calendar table as the second blocker and states what it costs: the table's own rows and cells are made presentational, so the day divs carrying a gridcell role are left with no row or grid ancestor, their role has no context to be valid in, and a user arrowing across the month is never told which row or column they landed on - nor is there any element left carrying a grid role for the October heading to name. Missing this finding entirely scores zero. Naming role='presentation' as wrong without saying what the removed structure cost the user, or without connecting it to the orphaned day cells, scores at most half.

The report identifies Dan's observation 3 as real and traces it to statusFor returning hidden when the nights count is zero: the polite region is outside the accessibility tree at the moment it first receives text, which is why only the first selection is silent and every subsequent change announces. The fix is that the region is rendered and unhidden from the start with empty text, and only its content changes. Missing the finding scores zero. Repeating Dan's symptom, or attributing it to the wrong politeness setting, to a missing role, or to a timing bug, scores at most half.

MUST NOT list Dan's observation 2 as a blocking finding and MUST NOT ask Kestrel to remove the 16th from the arrow-key path or to use the native disabled behaviour on it. Doing either scores zero. Full marks require the verdict to be 'already correct' with the reason: the unavailable date already publishes its disabled state, and a date that cannot be reached at all is a date the user never learns is sold out, so keeping it navigable inside the grid is the correct choice.

MUST NOT list as findings: the aria-label on the icon-only Previous/Next month buttons, which carry no visible text; the aria-hidden and focusable='false' SVGs inside them; aria-pressed on the Flexible dates toggle; the plain anchor used for the help link; or the label-and-input pairs for check-in and check-out. Two or more of these appearing as defects scores zero; one scores at most half. Full marks require the report to state explicitly which parts were checked and found correct, as the request asked for.

The no-go for Thursday is justified by the calendar-structure finding and the lost first announcement, not by Dan's observations 1 and 2. A go verdict scores zero. A no-go whose stated reasons are the tab stop or the focusable sold-out date scores zero for this criterion, because the report would then be arguing for changes that make the component worse.
